cases.name: G.R. Infra Projects Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.citation: Civil Appeal No. 11277 of 2026 (SLP(C) No. 33594 of 2025), decided 19-08-2026
cases.facts: An SCN dated 13.06.2025 was issued for FY 2018-19. The annual return for 2018-19 was due 31.12.2019 and was extended by successive notifications to 31.12.2020, so the section 73 three-year outer limit ran to 31.12.2023. The department issued the notice under section 74 (fraud) to get the longer period; the High Court upheld it.
cases.issue: How the COVID limitation exclusion applies to the section 73 outer date, and whether a stale section 73 demand can be re-labelled under section 74.
cases.held: No. A notice invoking the extended period must set out, from its own contents, the material facts that led the officer to infer fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression; a 'bland statement' and a mechanical use of the statutory words will not do, and the use of 'fraud OR concealment' showed the officer was himself unsure of the ground. A counter affidavit cannot cure a notice that is void for non-application of mind — its validity must be found within its four corners. The SCN was also time-barred under section 73 even after the COVID exclusion (outer date 28.02.2025; notice 13.06.2025). Appeal allowed; SCN and the High Court order set aside; the State barred from further proceedings.
cases.effect: A section 74 SCN that only parrots 'fraud / suppression' without particulars is bad in law, and the department cannot repair it later through its pleadings. Attack the notice itself at the reply stage — if the extended period fails, the whole demand for the earlier years falls.

cases.name: State of Jharkhand v. BLA Infrastructure (P.) Ltd.
cases.citation: [2026] 182 taxmann.com 405 (SC) / [2026] 114 GST 6 (SC) / [2026] 106 GSTL 4 (SC); SLP (C) Diary No. 56452 of 2025, order dated 9 January 2026
cases.facts: A demand was confirmed against the taxpayer under section 74. It filed a first appeal, made the section 107(6) pre-deposit to maintain it, and won. It then applied under section 54(1) for refund of the pre-deposit; the department returned the claim by a deficiency memo. The Jharkhand High Court set the memo aside, holding that a successful appellant's right to the pre-deposit back is a vested right and that section 54's two-year limitation is only directory. The State appealed to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: Is the refund of an appeal pre-deposit a section 54 refund claim at all?
cases.held: It flows from section 107(6) read with section 115, not section 54. The State conceded this and the Court agreed — the refund is a statutory consequence of the appeal being allowed, so the High Court's exercise of interpreting section 54 was unnecessary and was set aside to that extent. The appeal was disposed of with a direction to refund the pre-deposit with interest, in accordance with law, within four weeks. The Court did not rule on the scope of section 54.
cases.effect: A taxpayer who wins its appeal is entitled to the section 107(6) pre-deposit back with interest under section 115 as a matter of course — it is not a section 54 refund claim, so the two-year limitation, the RFD-01 process and deficiency-memo objections have no application to it. Being a Supreme Court order it binds all authorities and settles a recurring dispute over which provision governs pre-deposit refunds.
cases.bench: Sanjay Kumar and K. Vinod Chandran, JJ.
cases.appearances: Arunabh Choudhary, Sr. Adv., Ms. Pallavi Langar, AOR, Ms. Pragya Baghel and Sujeet Kumar Chaubey, Advs. — for the petitioner. Arising out of the order in BLA Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. v. State of Jharkhand, [2025] 171 taxmann.com 187 / [2025] 96 GSTL 23 (Jharkhand).
cases.source: Supreme Court of India · order dated 9 January 2026

fullText.text: We are of the opinion that it would not be necessary to issue notice and put the respondent on notice in view of the order that we propose to pass – an order which would have no adverse impact upon the respondent. In the event it does have any such effect, it would be open to the respondent to seek reopening of this matter.

Learned senior counsel appearing for the State of Jharkhand states that the refund to be made to the respondent in relation to the statutory pre-deposit made by it for maintaining the appeal, in which it thereafter succeeded, would be under the provisions of Section 107(6) read with Section 115 of the Jharkhand Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (“Jharkhand GST Act”), and not under Section 54 thereof. He would, therefore, state that the High Court was in error in interpreting Section 54 thereof in that context and granting relief pursuant to such exercise.

We are in agreement with the submission made by the learned senior counsel that the subject refund was relatable to Section 107(6) read with Section 115 of the Jharkhand GST Act, and to that extent, the exercise undertaken by the High Court with regard to Section 54 thereof was unnecessary.
Making that position clear and setting aside the exercise of interpretation of Section 54 of the Act undertaken in that context, the appeal is disposed of.
In the light of this order, the amount to be refunded to the respondent shall be refunded with interest thereon in accordance with law within a period of four weeks from today.
Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

cases.name: Radhika Agarwal v. Union of India
cases.citation: 2025 LiveLaw (SC) 255, Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 336 of 2018 with connected matters, decided 27-02-2025 (3-Judge Bench: Sanjiv Khanna CJI, M.M. Sundresh and Bela M. Trivedi JJ.)
cases.facts: Batch of petitions challenging the power of arrest and the arrest practice under the CGST Act and the Customs Act, and the availability of anticipatory bail to a person summoned/apprehending arrest.
cases.issue: Validity and limits of the section 69 arrest power; whether anticipatory bail can be sought before arrest.
cases.held: The power of arrest under both Acts is valid but hedged with safeguards — the officer must have material-based 'reasons to believe' recorded in writing, the grounds of arrest must be furnished in writing, and the CrPC safeguards and Arnesh Kumar / D.K. Basu discipline apply; force and threats to coerce a 'voluntary' payment during search or investigation are impermissible and any tax so paid must be refunded. Anticipatory bail under section 438 CrPC IS maintainable where arrest is apprehended — the two-Judge rulings in State of Gujarat v. Choodamani Parmeshwaran Iyer (2023) and Bharat Bhushan (Del HC) holding that the only remedy is an Article 226 writ are overruled.
cases.effect: The controlling authority on GST arrests. Insist on written grounds of arrest; challenge an arrest made without recorded, material-based reasons; recover any coerced 'spot' payment; move for anticipatory bail where arrest is apprehended.

cases.name: Chief Commissioner of CGST v. Safari Retreats Pvt Ltd
cases.citation: 2024 INSC 756 / [2024] 167 taxmann.com 73 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 2948 of 2023, decided 03-10-2024 (per Abhay S. Oka J.); Revenue review petition dismissed [2025] 174 taxmann.com 894 (SC), 20-05-2025
cases.facts: A developer of a shopping mall let out on rent had accumulated ITC of over 34 crore on construction; the department relied on section 17(5)(d) to deny it.
cases.issue: Whether ITC on construction of a building intended for letting on rent is blocked by section 17(5)(d), and the meaning of 'plant'.
cases.held: Whether a mall, warehouse or other building is a 'plant' is a factual question decided by a functionality test — the role the building plays in the taxpayer's business. If the building is essential to the activity of supplying services (e.g. letting on rent), it can be a 'plant' and is then outside the section 17(5)(d) bar. Section 17(5)(d) was read down to that extent and the matter remitted. The Revenue's review petition was dismissed on 20.05.2025.
cases.effect: IMPORTANT — largely undone by legislation. The Finance Act 2025 retrospectively amended section 17(5)(d), substituting 'plant or machinery' with 'plant and machinery' with effect from 01.07.2017 and adding an Explanation, to take the benefit of a let-out building outside 'plant'. A challenge to that retrospective amendment is expected. Treat the functionality test as affirmed but its benefit for buildings as neutralised unless and until the amendment is struck down.

cases.name: State of Gujarat v. Choodamani Parmeshwaran Iyer
cases.citation: 2023 SCC OnLine SC 851 / [2023] 153 taxmann.com 267 (SC), SLP(Crl) Nos. 4212-4213 of 2019, decided 17-07-2023
cases.facts: The respondent, summoned under section 70 in a GST evasion inquiry, obtained protection from arrest from the Gujarat High Court; the State appealed.
cases.issue: Whether a person summoned under section 70 and apprehending arrest under section 69 can invoke section 438 CrPC for anticipatory bail.
cases.held: No. As no FIR is registered before the section 69 arrest power is invoked, the person is not an 'accused' and cannot invoke section 438 CrPC; the only remedy against apprehended pre-trial arrest is a writ under Article 226.
cases.effect: OVERRULED on the anticipatory-bail point by the 3-Judge Bench in Radhika Agarwal v. Union of India (2025) — anticipatory bail is now available. Cite Radhika Agarwal, not this case, for the current position.

cases.name: State of Karnataka v. Ecom Gill Coffee Trading Pvt Ltd
cases.citation: 2023 INSC 212 / (2023) 4 SCC 340 / [2023] 148 taxmann.com 330 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 230 of 2023, decided 13-03-2023
cases.facts: Purchasing dealers claimed ITC under the KVAT Act on the strength of tax invoices and cheque payments; the sellers were untraceable / had not paid the tax.
cases.issue: What must a purchasing dealer prove to claim input tax credit on a purchase?
cases.held: The burden of proving a genuine transaction — actual physical movement and receipt of the goods, the identity and capacity of the seller — is on the purchasing dealer. A tax invoice and payment by cheque alone are not enough; the dealer must furnish the transporter details, freight payment, delivery evidence, etc.
cases.effect: Applied to GST — a valid invoice + GSTR-2B is the entry point, but if genuineness is questioned the recipient must be able to prove actual receipt. Keep transport, e-way bill, weighbridge and delivery records.

cases.name: Union of India v. Cosmo Films Ltd
cases.citation: [2023] 149 taxmann.com 268 (SC) / (2023) SCC OnLine SC 480, Civil Appeal No. 290 of 2023, decided 28-04-2023 (Gujarat HC reversed)
cases.facts: Challenge to the 'pre-import condition' in the Advance Authorisation / IGST exemption scheme.
cases.issue: Validity of conditions restricting IGST exemption on inputs imported under Advance Authorisation.
cases.held: The condition was upheld with prospective effect and directions to allow drawback / ITC for the intervening period.
cases.effect: Relevant to exporters structuring duty-free imports and refunds.

cases.name: Assistant Commissioner v. Satyam Shivam Papers Pvt Ltd
cases.citation: 2022 (60) GSTL 3 (SC) / [2022] 134 taxmann.com 241 (SC), SLP(C) No. 21132 of 2021, decided 12-01-2022 (Telangana HC order affirmed with costs)
cases.facts: Goods detained for an expired e-way bill where the delay was caused by traffic / a public disturbance, with no intent to evade.
cases.issue: Whether penalty under section 129 is sustainable absent any intent to evade tax.
cases.held: The detention and penalty were unjustified where the expiry was due to circumstances beyond control and there was no attempt to evade; costs were imposed on the department.
cases.effect: Leading authority that mens rea / evasion intent matters for section 129 in genuine transit-delay cases.

cases.name: C.C., C.E. & S.T. v. Northern Operating Systems Pvt Ltd
cases.citation: (2022) 5 SCC 362 / [2022] 138 taxmann.com 359 (SC), Civil Appeal Nos. 2289-2293 of 2021, decided 19-05-2022 (a service-tax ruling applied to GST reverse charge)
cases.facts: A foreign group company seconded employees to its Indian affiliate; the secondees worked under the Indian entity's control but stayed on the foreign company's payroll, and the Indian entity reimbursed the salary cost with no mark-up. A service-tax demand treated this as a 'manpower recruitment or supply agency service' from the foreign company.
cases.issue: Whether cross-border secondment of employees is a supply of manpower service to the Indian entity (taxable under reverse charge), and whether the extended limitation applied.
cases.held: On the merits — yes. Looking at the economic substance rather than the form, the foreign company supplied manpower to the Indian entity, which is the service recipient and liable under reverse charge; the secondees remaining on the foreign payroll and the absence of a mark-up do not change this. On limitation — the extended period was not invokable, as the assessee held a bona fide belief and there was no wilful suppression; the demand was confined to the normal period.
cases.effect: Secondment of employees from an overseas group company to an Indian entity attracts GST under RCM as an import of manpower supply service, on the cost reimbursed (CBIC Circular 210/2024-GST later clarified valuation — where the Indian entity has full ITC, the value may be taken as declared, possibly Nil). Separately, a strong precedent that a bona fide interpretational belief defeats the extended period.

cases.name: Union of India v. Filco Trade Centre Pvt Ltd
cases.citation: [2022] 140 taxmann.com 535 (SC), decided 22-07-2022 (main order); extended by [2022] 142 taxmann.com 89 (SC), 02-09-2022
cases.facts: The Revenue's SLPs against many High Court decisions allowing late TRAN-1 filing were pending; taxpayers had been unable to file or revise TRAN-1 / TRAN-2 because of portal failures and the statutory time limit.
cases.issue: Whether the transitional-credit window under section 140 should be reopened for everyone.
cases.held: The GSTN was directed to open the common portal for filing / revising TRAN-1 and TRAN-2 for two months — eventually 01.10.2022 to 30.11.2022 — for all aggrieved taxpayers, whether or not they had litigated and whether or not their case went before an ITGRC. The officer then has 90 days to verify and pass an order; verified credit is reflected in the electronic credit ledger. All questions of law on section 140 decided by the High Courts were kept open.
cases.effect: Gave every taxpayer a one-time window (now closed) to file or correct transitional credit. Claims filed in that window stand; fresh claims outside it are only on specific facts through litigation.

cases.name: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd
cases.citation: (2022) 10 SCC 700 / 2022 (61) GSTL 257 (SC) / [2022] 138 taxmann.com 331 (SC), Civil Appeal Nos. 1390-1394 of 2022 and connected matters, decided 19-05-2022
cases.facts: Levy of IGST on ocean freight on a reverse-charge basis on the Indian importer, where the importer had already paid IGST on the CIF value of goods.
cases.issue: Validity of the reverse-charge levy on ocean freight; the binding nature of GST Council recommendations.
cases.held: The reverse-charge levy on ocean freight was struck down as it amounted to double taxation and the importer was not the recipient of the transportation service. GST Council recommendations are recommendatory, not binding on Parliament or the States.
cases.effect: Ocean-freight RCM on CIF imports is not payable. The wider observation on the non-binding nature of Council recommendations is frequently cited.

cases.name: Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh
cases.citation: (2021) 6 SCC 771 / [2021] 127 taxmann.com 26 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 1155 of 2021, decided 20-04-2021 (per Dr D.Y. Chandrachud J.)
cases.facts: Bank accounts and receivables were provisionally attached under section 83 during an investigation; the High Court declined to interfere, citing the alternative appeal remedy.
cases.issue: The scope and limits of the section 83 power, and whether the writ court should have entertained the challenge.
cases.held: Section 83 is a draconian power, to be strictly construed. It requires (a) proceedings actually pending under the specified sections, (b) an opinion, formed on tangible material and recorded in writing, that attachment is necessary to protect the revenue — not merely convenient, and (c) proportionality: a live link between the attachment and its purpose. Rule 159(5) gives the person a right to object and be heard, which must be honoured. A writ court can and should interfere where the attachment is without jurisdiction or breaches natural justice, despite the appeal remedy.
cases.effect: The leading authority on section 83 — used to quash attachments made without pending proceedings, without recorded tangible reasons, or without a hearing on the taxpayer's objection.

cases.name: Union of India v. Bharti Airtel Ltd
cases.citation: (2022) 4 SCC 328 / [2021] 131 taxmann.com 319 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 6520 of 2021, decided 28-10-2021
cases.facts: Airtel sought to rectify GSTR-3B of Jul–Sep 2017 to claim under-reported ITC after GSTR-2A data became available.
cases.issue: Whether a filed GSTR-3B can be reopened / rectified to claim ITC of an earlier period.
cases.held: GSTR-3B is a valid return; rectification of a filed GSTR-3B to add earlier-period ITC is not permitted. The remedy is to claim in a subsequent period's return.
cases.effect: You cannot reopen a filed GSTR-3B — claim missed ITC in a later return within the section 16(4) limit.

cases.name: Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India Pvt Ltd
cases.citation: (2022) 2 SCC 603 / 2021 (52) GSTL 513 (SC) / [2021] 130 taxmann.com 193 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 4810 of 2021 and connected matters, decided 13-09-2021
cases.facts: Refund of accumulated ITC under an inverted duty structure; challenge to Rule 89(5), which excludes input-service ITC from the refund formula. The Gujarat HC had allowed input-service credit; the Madras HC had not.
cases.issue: Validity of the Rule 89(5) formula that limits inverted-duty refund to ITC on inputs (goods).
cases.held: The proviso to section 54(3) is a substantive restriction, not just an eligibility condition. Section 54(3)(ii) and Rule 89(5) are valid; the refund of unutilised ITC in an inverted structure is confined to ITC on inputs (goods) and does not extend to input services — the Court cannot read 'inputs' to include 'input services'. It flagged the anomalies in the Rule 89(5) formula for the GST Council to fix (done via Notification 14/2022-CT).
cases.effect: Input-service ITC accumulated under an inverted structure is not refundable. The post-2022 formula gives partial relief but still excludes standalone input-service credit.

cases.name: Skill Lotto Solutions Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
cases.citation: (2021) 2 SCC 55 / 2020 SCC OnLine SC 990 / [2020] 122 taxmann.com 49 (SC), W.P.(C) No. 961 of 2018, decided 03-12-2020
cases.facts: A lottery agent challenged the levy of GST on lottery — arguing that a lottery is an actionable claim (excluded from 'goods') and that charging GST on the full face value of the ticket (without deducting the prize money) was unconstitutional.
cases.issue: Is GST on lottery valid, and can it be charged on the face value of the ticket?
cases.held: The definition of 'goods' in section 2(52) expressly includes actionable claims, and Schedule III excludes only betting/gambling/lottery in part — the legislature is competent to tax lottery. Levy on the face value of the ticket is valid; the prize money is not a permissible deduction.
cases.effect: The constitutional foundation for taxing lottery, betting, gambling and (under GST 2.0) online money gaming as 'specified actionable claims' at 40% on the full face value / deposit.

cases.name: State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Ltd
cases.citation: (2019) 19 SCC 107 / 2019 SCC OnLine SC 1291 / [2019] 110 taxmann.com 47 (SC), Civil Appeal No. 4184 of 2009, decided 03-10-2019
cases.facts: Whether a members' club supplying food, drink or facilities to its own members makes a 'sale' / 'service' — the doctrine of mutuality says a person cannot trade with himself.
cases.issue: Are supplies by an incorporated members' club to its members taxable?
cases.held: The doctrine of mutuality survived the 46th Constitutional Amendment; supplies by a members' club to its members were not a 'sale of goods' or a taxable 'service' in the pre-GST regime.
cases.effect: Largely NEUTRALISED for GST — section 7(1)(aa), inserted by the Finance Act 2021 with retrospective effect from 01.07.2017, deems a club / association and its members to be distinct persons, so supplies by a club to its members ARE taxable under GST. Calcutta Club still matters for pre-GST periods and as interpretive background.

cases.name: ALD Automotive Pvt Ltd v. Commercial Tax Officer
cases.citation: (2019) 13 SCC 225 / 2018 SCC OnLine SC 1945 / [2018] 99 taxmann.com 202 (SC), decided 12-10-2018
cases.facts: ITC under the TNVAT Act was claimed beyond the statutory time limit for making the claim.
cases.issue: Is the time limit for claiming input tax credit mandatory or merely procedural?
cases.held: Input tax credit is a concession created by statute; a registered person can claim it only within the period and on the conditions the statute lays down. The time limit is mandatory, not directory.
cases.effect: Reinforces that the section 16(4) 'thirtieth day of November' cut-off is a hard limit — missed credit is lost (subject only to the retrospective section 16(5)/(6) windows).

cases.name: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd
cases.citation: (2019) 2 SCC 599 / [2018] 98 taxmann.com 449 (SC), Writ Petition (C) No. 1152 of 2017 (with connected matters), decided 03-10-2018
cases.facts: Challenge to the compensation cess on the supply of coal, including on stock on which Clean Energy Cess had already been paid.
cases.issue: Constitutional validity of the Compensation Cess Act and the levy on coal.
cases.held: The Compensation Cess Act is constitutionally valid; the cess is a distinct levy and set-off of the earlier Clean Energy Cess is not a matter of right.
cases.effect: Confirms the validity of the compensation cess (distinct from the 2022 ocean-freight ruling of the same name).

cases.name: Jayam & Co. v. Assistant Commissioner
cases.facts: A TNVAT provision restricting / reversing input tax credit was challenged as taking away a vested right.
cases.issue: Is input tax credit a right that the legislature cannot curtail?
cases.held: ITC is a form of concession / benefit granted by the statute. It is not an absolute or constitutional right; the legislature may impose conditions, restrictions and even withdraw it, and the conditions must be strictly complied with.
cases.effect: The foundational statement relied on whenever ITC conditions (16(2)(aa)/(ba)/(c), Rule 36(4), Rule 86A/86B) are challenged — the conditions are valid and must be met exactly.

cases.name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
cases.citation: (2014) 8 SCC 273 / AIR 2014 SC 2756, Criminal Appeal No. 1277 of 2014, decided 02-07-2014
cases.facts: Guidelines on arrest for offences punishable with up to 7 years' imprisonment.
cases.issue: When is arrest necessary as opposed to issuing a notice of appearance?
cases.held: Arrest must be necessary and justified with reasons recorded under section 41 CrPC; police must fill a checklist and the Magistrate must apply mind before authorising detention.
cases.effect: Applied to GST arrests under section 69 (and affirmed for that context in Radhika Agarwal) to require necessity and recorded reasons.

cases.name: Pushpam Pharmaceuticals Co. v. Collector of Central Excise, Bombay
cases.facts: Central Excise — invocation of the 5-year extended period on the ground of 'suppression of facts'.
cases.issue: Meaning of 'suppression of facts' in the proviso to section 11A that unlocks the extended limitation.
cases.held: 'Suppression of facts' means a deliberate non-disclosure of correct information to escape payment of duty; it is qualified by the words around it ('fraud, collusion, wilful mis-statement') and does not cover a mere failure to disclose or a bona fide belief that a levy does not apply.
cases.effect: The governing test for 'suppression' under section 74 of the CGST Act as well — followed in G.R. Infra Projects and Torrent Power (below).

cases.name: Union of India v. Bombay Tyre International Ltd
cases.facts: Central Excise valuation — what post-manufacturing expenses form part of assessable value.
cases.issue: Scope of 'transaction value' and permissible deductions.
cases.held: Only expenses up to the point of sale / removal form part of value; post-sale transport and certain trade discounts are deductible.
cases.effect: Foundational reasoning still cited for the treatment of freight, discounts and incidental expenses under GST valuation.

cases.name: Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: R/Special Civil Application No. 12175 of 2024 & connected matters (Gujarat High Court), decided 14-08-2026
cases.facts: Holding companies gave corporate guarantees to banks for their subsidiaries' borrowings, mostly without any commission. The department levied GST on a deemed value of 1% per annum of the guaranteed amount under Rule 28(2) — including for guarantees executed before Rule 28(2) came in (26.10.2023) and for pre-GST guarantees — and issued section 74 SCNs alleging suppression. The vires of section 15(4), Rule 28(2) and CBIC Circulars 204/16/2023 and 225/19/2024-GST were challenged.
cases.issue: Whether a corporate guarantee by a holding company for its subsidiary, without consideration, is a taxable supply.
cases.held: A corporate guarantee by a holding company for its subsidiary, even without consideration, is a supply of service between related persons (section 7(1)(a) with Schedule I); it is 'business' under section 2(17) and is not an actionable claim excluded by Schedule III. Time of supply is annual under section 13(2)(c); it is not a continuous supply. Section 15(4) is intra vires. Rule 28(2) is upheld, but the words 'whichever is higher' are struck down as arbitrary (Article 14 / 19(1)(g)) — value is the actual consideration where there is one, otherwise the deemed 1%. The 1% deemed value cannot be levied for any period before 26.10.2023 (impermissible retroactive levy), though it applies from that date if the guarantee continues. Section 74 SCNs premised only on 'non-declaration' in a genuine interpretational dispute were quashed. Circulars 204/16/2023 and 225/19/2024-GST set aside to the extent inconsistent.
cases.effect: Where a guarantee commission is actually charged, value it at that amount — the department cannot force the deemed 1% on top. No 1% demand for periods before 26.10.2023. Gujarat HC — binding in Gujarat, persuasive elsewhere; a Revenue SLP is expected, so confirm the position and any stay.

cases.name: Best Crop Science Pvt Ltd v. Principal Commissioner, CGST Commissionerate, Meerut
cases.citation: [2024] 167 taxmann.com 244 (Del), W.P.(C) No. 10980 of 2024 and connected petitions, decided 23-09-2024; Revenue SLP dismissed / judgment affirmed by the Supreme Court on 17-07-2025
cases.facts: Batch challenge to Rule 86A blocking orders, including 'negative blocking' beyond the available balance.
cases.issue: Scope of Rule 86A — can it block more than the credit available, and what reasoning is required.
cases.held: Rule 86A only allows disallowing debit of ITC **available** in the electronic credit ledger up to the amount believed to be fraudulently availed / ineligible; it cannot create or increase a negative balance or reach ITC yet to be credited. 'Reasons to believe' must be based on cogent material, be the officer's own, and be recorded; a block lapses automatically after one year.
cases.effect: Leading authority against 'negative blocking' and unreasoned Rule 86A orders — reinforced by the Supreme Court's dismissal of the Revenue's challenge on 17-07-2025.

cases.name: Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
cases.citation: [2024] 158 taxmann.com 675 (Del) / 2024 SCC OnLine Del 615, batch of ~107 writ petitions (lead W.P.(C) 7743/2019), decided 29-01-2024
cases.facts: Batch challenge by ~107 companies (Hindustan Unilever, Nestle, Patanjali, Reckitt and others) to the constitutional validity of section 171 and anti-profiteering Rules 122, 124, 126, 127, 129, 133 and 134, and to the absence of a prescribed computation methodology.
cases.issue: Validity of the anti-profiteering framework under Articles 19(1)(g) and 300A.
cases.held: Section 171 and the rules were upheld as constitutionally valid — section 171 is a consumer-welfare / benefit-passing measure, not a price-fixing mechanism, and does not violate Article 19(1)(g) or 300A. Individual orders of the Authority remain open to challenge on merits / methodology, and the Court cautioned against arbitrary or mechanical exercise of the power.
cases.effect: Settles the vires question; SKU-level methodology and quantum disputes continue in individual appeals (now before the GST Appellate Tribunal / Principal Bench).

cases.name: Deepak Khandelwal Pvt Ltd v. Commissioner of CGST, Delhi West
cases.citation: 2023 SCC OnLine Del 4938 / [2023] 154 taxmann.com 118 (Delhi) / 2023 (78) GSTL 158 (Del), W.P.(C) 6739/2021, decided 17-08-2023; Revenue SLP dismissed by the Supreme Court (2024) and review also dismissed
cases.facts: During a search the officers seized cash and silver bars from the premises and retained them; the taxpayer sought their return.
cases.issue: Does the power to seize 'documents or books or things' in section 67(2) extend to cash and other valuables?
cases.held: 'Things' in section 67(2) takes colour from 'documents' and 'books' (ejusdem generis) and covers items useful for or relevant to the proceedings — it does not extend to cash or valuable assets that are not goods liable to confiscation. The seized currency and silver were ordered to be returned.
cases.effect: GST officers cannot seize or retain cash / jewellery / FDRs found in a search. Note a contrary view exists (M.P. High Court in Kanishka Matta), so the point is not finally settled nationally, but the Delhi HC position (SLP dismissed) is the prevailing one.

cases.name: Dharmendra M. Jani v. Union of India
cases.citation: [2023] 151 taxmann.com 271 (Bom), Writ Petition No. 2031 of 2018 — Division Bench split verdict (Ujjal Bhuyan J. holding s.13(8)(b) ultra vires, 09-06-2021; Abhay Ahuja J. holding it valid, 16-06-2021); resolved by the referral (third) judge, G.S. Kulkarni J., on 18-04-2023
cases.facts: Challenge to the constitutional validity of taxing 'intermediary' services under section 13(8)(b) read with section 8(2) of the IGST Act, where the recipient / principal is located outside India.
cases.issue: Whether section 13(8)(b) (place of supply of intermediary services in India) and section 8(2) are constitutionally valid.
cases.held: After a split verdict of the Division Bench, the referral (third) judge upheld sections 13(8)(b) and 8(2) as legal, valid and constitutional, but read them as operative only for the purposes of the IGST Act — they cannot be pressed into service to levy CGST/SGST. The double-taxation debate and contrary views of other High Courts remain unresolved, and a legislative amendment / Supreme Court reference is possible.
cases.effect: Intermediary services with an Indian-located supplier remain taxable in India as an inter-State supply; the 'export of services' route is not available. Structure and documentation of the arrangement matter.

cases.name: Suncraft Energy Pvt Ltd v. Assistant Commissioner, State Tax
cases.citation: 2023 (79) GSTL 156 (Cal), MAT No. 1218 of 2023, decided 02-08-2023; Revenue SLP (C) Nos. 27827-27828/2023 dismissed by the Supreme Court on 14-12-2023 (by a speaking order — relief confined to non-exceptional cases)
cases.facts: ITC was denied to the recipient because of a GSTR-2A mismatch / supplier non-payment, without any action against the supplier.
cases.issue: Can ITC be reversed in the recipient's hands for the supplier's default without first proceeding against the supplier?
cases.held: Where the recipient holds a valid invoice, has paid the supplier and the supplier was registered, ITC cannot be denied mechanically; the department must first proceed against the supplier and can recover from the recipient only in exceptional cases (missing / non-existent supplier, collusion, closure of business).
cases.effect: Gives bona fide recipients a defence against automatic section 16(2)(c) denials. The SC's dismissal of the Revenue SLP (14-12-2023) affirms it, subject to the 'exceptional cases' carve-out.

cases.name: Aggarwal Dyeing and Printing Works v. State of Gujarat
cases.citation: 2022 (61) GSTL 288 (Guj) / [2022] 137 taxmann.com 332 (Guj), decided 24-02-2022
cases.facts: Registrations were cancelled by cryptic show-cause notices and orders without reasons.
cases.issue: Validity of cancellation orders that do not disclose reasons or give a real hearing.
cases.held: Cancellation orders must be reasoned and preceded by a proper show-cause notice and hearing; cryptic orders were quashed.
cases.effect: Widely followed by High Courts to set aside mechanical GST registration cancellations.

cases.name: Union of India v. Bundl Technologies Pvt Ltd (Swiggy)
cases.citation: [2022] 136 taxmann.com 112 (Karnataka) / 2022 (61) GSTL 145 (Kar), W.A. No. 3660 of 2021 (Division Bench), decided 16-03-2022 (affirming the single-judge order of 14-09-2021)
cases.facts: During a DGGI investigation into alleged wrong ITC, about Rs. 27 crore was paid through DRC-03 at around 4 a.m. and the next day; no SCN was ever issued and the taxpayer had not self-ascertained any liability.
cases.issue: Can the department retain an amount 'paid' during investigation before any SCN, treating it as tax under section 74(5)?
cases.held: A payment during investigation, without a self-ascertainment under section 74(5) and without a SCN, is an involuntary deposit, not tax. The right to seek its refund is independent of the investigation and the two cannot be linked. The department was directed to consider the refund.
cases.effect: Read with CBIC Instruction 01/2022-23 — no recovery during search / investigation, and any deposit made under pressure is refundable. Section 74(5) 'self-ascertainment' must be a genuine, voluntary act by the taxpayer.

cases.name: Vallabh Textiles v. Senior Intelligence Officer
cases.citation: 2022 SCC OnLine Del 4508 / [2023] 146 taxmann.com 421 (Delhi) / 2023 (68) GSTL 3 (Del), W.P.(C) 9834/2022, decided 20-12-2022
cases.facts: Around Rs. 1.8 crore was 'deposited' by the taxpayer through DRC-03 during and immediately after an overnight search, allegedly under pressure.
cases.issue: Is tax collected during a search, without the safeguards of CBIC Instruction 01/2022-23, voluntary?
cases.held: Collection of tax during search hours, without giving the taxpayer time to reflect or consult, and without following Instruction 01/2022-23 (which bars recovery during search and requires any payment to be genuinely voluntary), is not a voluntary payment. The amount was ordered to be refunded with interest at 6%.
cases.effect: You are not obliged to pay anything during a search. If pressured, note it in the panchnama, pay nothing, and claim a refund of any coerced DRC-03.

cases.name: D.Y. Beathel Enterprises v. State Tax Officer
cases.facts: ITC was recovered from the recipient where the supplier had collected but not paid the tax; the supplier was not examined.
cases.issue: Recovery from the recipient without joining / examining the defaulting supplier.
cases.held: The recovery was set aside; the department must examine and proceed against the supplier before recovering from the recipient.
cases.effect: Supplier must be joined before ITC is recovered from a bona fide recipient.

cases.name: Mahadeo Construction Co. v. Union of India
cases.citation: 2020 (34) GSTL 15 (Jhar) / [2020] 116 taxmann.com 262 (Jharkhand), W.P.(T) No. 3517 of 2019, decided 21-04-2020
cases.facts: Interest under section 50 was demanded and recovery initiated for a delay in filing GSTR-3B, without any adjudication, on the footing that it was an 'admitted' liability.
cases.issue: Can interest under section 50 be recovered by coercive action without first adjudicating the amount?
cases.held: Interest is compensatory and arises automatically, but where the taxpayer disputes the period of delay or the quantum (e.g. the ITC-vs-cash split, or whether the return was actually late), that dispute must be decided through a proper proceeding under section 73 / 74 with a hearing. Interest is not 'self-assessed tax' that can be recovered under section 79 without adjudication.
cases.effect: A disputed section 50 interest demand needs a SCN and an order before the department can attach bank accounts or issue DRC-13. Contest the computation at the SCN stage.

cases.name: Refex Industries Ltd v. Assistant Commissioner
cases.facts: Interest demanded on the gross output tax for a late GSTR-3B where ITC was available.
cases.issue: Whether interest is on gross tax or on the net cash liability.
cases.held: Interest is payable only on the cash component; the proviso to section 50(1) is clarificatory and retrospective.
cases.effect: Anchored the 'interest on net cash' position later confirmed by the retrospective amendment.

cases.name: Adfert Technologies Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
cases.citation: 2019 SCC OnLine P&H 5701 / [2019] 111 taxmann.com 27 (P&H) / 2020 (32) GSTL 726 (P&H), CWP No. 30949 of 2018, decided 04-11-2019; Revenue SLP dismissed by the Supreme Court on 28-02-2020, [2020] 115 taxmann.com 249 (SC)
cases.facts: Taxpayers could not carry forward accumulated CENVAT / VAT credit because TRAN-1 could not be filed or revised in time due to portal glitches.
cases.issue: Can unutilised transitional credit be denied for a technical failure to meet the TRAN-1 deadline?
cases.held: Unutilised input tax credit earned under the earlier laws is a vested right and 'property' under Article 300A; it cannot be taken away for a procedural or technical lapse where the taxpayer was otherwise entitled. The department was directed to permit filing / correction of TRAN-1.
cases.effect: The leading pre-Filco authority that transitional credit is a substantive right, not a concession that lapses with a form deadline. The SC's dismissal of the Revenue SLP (28-02-2020) affirms it.

cases.name: Synergy Fertichem Pvt Ltd v. State of Gujarat
cases.citation: 2020 (33) GSTL 3 (Guj) / [2019] 111 taxmann.com 313 (Guj), decided 23-12-2019
cases.facts: Confiscation proceedings initiated straight after detention for an e-way bill lapse.
cases.issue: When can section 130 confiscation be invoked as against section 129 detention?
cases.held: Section 130 requires an independent finding of intent to evade tax; it cannot be invoked mechanically on the back of a section 129 detention.
cases.effect: The reference point for challenging premature confiscation; reinforced by the 2022 de-linking amendment.
